title: Is This El Niño a 'Mega' One? Scientists Say Not So Fast
summary:
Godzilla has battled giant moths and three-headed dragons. But even the king of the monsters might have trouble keeping up with this year's El Niño. First came "Super El Niño." Then "Godzilla El Niño." Now there is a new monster in town: "Mega El Niño." But has this year's El Niño really been upgraded? Scientists say there is no official upgrade.

El Niño is a climate pattern that happens when unusually warm water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean changes how air moves around the world, shifting weather far and wide. Scientists measure its strength by averaging sea surface temperatures over three months in a large section of the Pacific.

The latest nickname gained attention after US meteorologist Ryan Maue posted a map online showing what he said were sea surface temperatures as much as 10 degrees Celsius above normal near Peru and the Galapagos Islands. "This is now a Mega El Niño," he wrote.

But the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, NOAA, tells a different story. Its analysis shows temperature differences of roughly 4 to 6 degrees Celsius in the eastern Pacific, said Michelle L'Heureux, NOAA's El Niño team lead. NOAA has not changed its wording: it classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong.

"As far as I can tell there's no reason to invent a new category above 'very strong' that we have right now," said Emily Becker, a research associate professor at the University of Miami. David Phillips, a climatologist emeritus with Environment and Climate Change Canada, disagreed: "Maybe 'Godzilla' is not strong enough for it." By NOAA's own measure, this year's El Niño has reached the highest classification, very strong, running on par with the events of 1997-98 and 2015-16. So is it a mega monster, or just a very strong El Niño with a very big nickname? For now, the official answer is very strong.
why_it_matters: El Niño changes weather around the world, so knowing how strong it really is helps people prepare for storms, rain and heat.

background_read: El Niño is a natural climate pattern in the Pacific Ocean that comes and goes over several years.
When the ocean warms up in the tropical Pacific, it can change winds and rainfall in many parts of the world.
Scientists watch ocean temperatures closely so they can warn people about storms, floods and droughts that El Niño can bring.
Different countries measure El Niño in slightly different ways, which is why experts can disagree about how strong one event is.
